name: Pedro Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out of the house by quarter to seven in my old silver hatchback, and my first call is Mr Haddad, who's eighty-eight and used to work on the railways. I get him up, washed, dressed and his porridge on, and I've got thirty minutes for that, which is never enough. Then it's six or seven more calls across the valley before lunch, and the agency, Brightpath, only pays for the time inside the houses, not the driving between them. I like the people. What wears me out is the clock, and the phone app that buzzes at me if I stay four minutes over.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: You tap in when you arrive and tap out when you leave, and it shows the office if you're late. I don't use it for anything else and I don't want to. I still write my notes in the paper folder at each house, because the families read those, and half my clients wouldn't know what to do with a screen. My partner Tomas says I'm stubborn about it, and he's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like now. The app came in, nothing got better, and I'm still driving the same lanes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the union branch meeting: the problem in care was never a lack of gadgets. It's fifteen-minute visits and pay that doesn't cover the petrol. If AI fizzles out, fine, but the work still needs fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I'm stuck exactly where I am, which isn't great either. Brightpath's council contract is up for renewal in the spring, and last time they renewed it they cut our mileage rate. I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank, so one bad month and I'm borrowing from Tomas again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds and I'd push harder in the union about paid travel time, because that's my real raise. I'd ask the coordinator for the Saturday double-up calls, the ones where two of us do a hoist, because they pay a bit more. And I'd stop buying lunch at the petrol station and bring sandwiches, which sounds small but it's about thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear about robots, it's the same low hum of worry about rent that's been there since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one bad month and you're borrowing. What would a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. It's got a hundred and sixty thousand on the clock and the clutch is going. If the clutch on my car goes, I can't work, because there's no bus that gets you to a farmhouse at seven in the morning. A clutch is maybe six hundred, and I don't have six hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the contract renewal went badly, what's your fallback around here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's one other agency within twenty miles and the hospital's porter jobs, and that's it. The other agency pays even less per visit. I'd stay put and fight for the contract terms, because moving isn't something Tomas and I could afford anyway.

say: I'd say care's real problem is **fifteen-minute visits**, not a lack of gadgets.
I'd tell the union branch that **paid travel time** matters more than any app.
think: Privately I think staying the same means staying **stuck on low pay**.
The **council contract renewal** in spring could cut my mileage rate again.
With about **two weeks' savings**, one car repair puts me in debt.
do: Push the union branch on **paid travel time** before the spring contract renewal.
Ask for **Saturday double-up calls**, which pay a little more per hour.
Bring packed lunches to save about **thirty a week** on petrol-station food.
feel: A **low, steady worry** about rent and the car, not about robots.
S0.quote: If the clutch on my car goes, I can't work, because there's no bus that gets you to a farmhouse at seven in the morning.
fieldNote: His worry in AI Plateau is **old money pressure**: a failing clutch, thin savings and a contract renewal.
He frames everything through the **union**, and blames contract terms rather than technology.
His dislike of the visit-logging app is **personal and stubborn**, and he admits it.

steps.text: Press the union branch for paid travel time before spring renewal
Take Saturday double-up hoist calls for the higher rate
Pack lunches instead of buying at the petrol station

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. So the office, the rota, the care plans. Not the washing and the hoisting, not yet anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the branch meeting that if the office gets cheaper, that money should come to the people on the road. That's the line I'd post too. Somebody's going to save a fortune on coordinators and it won't be us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the rota gets handed to a computer, and a computer will squeeze our visits tighter than any person ever did. Our coordinator Sandra knows my client Mrs Brennan needs an extra five minutes because of her dementia. Rota software won't care. I'll be the one tapping out late and getting the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Sandra and the other carers to write down every client who needs longer, before the new system comes in, so it's on record. I'd ask the union rep to get a clause that no visit is cut below thirty minutes by the software. I wouldn't learn the new system beyond what I have to, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, a bit. It feels like the one human in the office who understands the job gets replaced, and we get a stricter boss that never sleeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the new system. Could that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If they start judging us by how well we use it, I'd look bad next to the younger ones. But I'm twenty-seven, not sixty, so I'd learn the tapping and nothing else. The care is the job, the phone isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra. She's fifty-three and she's done that rota for eleven years. If they replace her with software, where does she go round here? Probably back on the road, and her knees won't take it.

say: I'd say office **savings from AI** should go to the carers on the road.
I'd post that someone will save a **fortune on coordinators**, and it won't be carers.
think: I think **rota software** will squeeze visits tighter than our coordinator Sandra ever did.
Software won't know which clients, like Mrs Brennan, **need extra minutes**.
I'll be the one getting **warnings for lateness** the computer caused.
do: Write down every client who **needs longer visits** before the new system starts.
Ask the union rep for a **thirty-minute minimum** the software can't cut.
Learn only the **app tapping** the agency requires, nothing more.
feel: **Angry** that the one office person who understands the job gets replaced.
S1.quote: Our coordinator Sandra knows my client Mrs Brennan needs an extra five minutes because of her dementia. Rota software won't care.
fieldNote: He expects AI to hit him **through the rota**, not by taking his hands-on work.
His first move is **collective**: documenting needs and asking for a contract clause.
He refuses to learn more than the minimum, and admits it may **cost him**.

steps.text: Record which clients need longer visits before the rota software arrives
Ask the union rep for a thirty-minute visit minimum clause
Keep doing rounds and learn only the required app taps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's 2028. And robots doing the hands-on stuff by 2031. I'd be thirty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say nobody is putting my clients in the hands of a machine without a fight. I'd be saying that in the branch, in the pub, everywhere. Older people deserve a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. The office goes in 2028, so the rota and the care plans and Sandra are gone straight away. Then I've got about three years before a robot can do the hoist and the shower, and I've got no savings, no other trade, and there's nothing else round here but the porter jobs, which a robot would probably take first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the union and push for a law that says personal care stays with people. I'd get on a list at the hospital for a porter or healthcare assistant job, just to have something else. And Tomas and I would cancel the holiday we've been saving for, and put that two hundred towards the car and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Those three years between 2028 and 2031: what changes in your day during them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The visits are still mine, but everything around them is a machine. The care plan's written by AI, the rota's AI, the families probably ask the AI how their mum is instead of reading my folder. I'd be doing the washing while something else decides how long I get to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas the night you hear the robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan B and I don't have one. Tomas works at the garden centre, and that's not exactly safe either. I think we'd sit at the kitchen table and just add up what we've got, which won't take long.

say: I'd say nobody puts my **clients with a machine** without a fight.
I'd say in the branch and the pub that older people deserve **a person** in the room.
think: Privately I'd be **scared**: the office and the coordinator go in 2028.
I'd have about **three years** before robots can hoist and shower clients.
I've **no savings** and no other trade in a valley with few jobs.
do: Push through the union for a **law keeping personal care** with people.
Join the hospital list for a **porter or healthcare assistant** job.
Cancel the holiday and put the **two hundred saved** towards car and rent.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a letter he knows is coming.
S2.quote: I'd be doing the washing while something else decides how long I get to do it.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as a slow squeeze, not a reprieve.
His public line is **defiant**, but privately he has no plan B.
His partner's **garden centre job** feels unsafe too, so the household has no backup.

steps.text: Campaign through the union for a law keeping personal care human
Apply to the hospital list for porter or healthcare assistant work
Cancel the holiday and move the two hundred to car and rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. Not by much, though, when you've got nothing put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the same as before: care should stay human, and the government should make sure of it. I'd add that five years is plenty of time to pass a law, so there's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years means I'd waste three of them hoping it won't happen. That's what I'm like, I know it. The office would go in 2031, and I'd be thirty-five when the robots come for the hands-on part in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to get my level three care diploma through the council's free course, because a better qualification might keep me on the complex cases longer. I'd put twenty a week away, even if it hurts. And I'd go to the meetings when the union starts campaigning, not just read the emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then worse as the date gets closer. Five years sounds long until you're in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the diploma, when you said you don't like learning new things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the diploma's about care, not about phones. Pressure sores, end-of-life care, the stuff I already half know. If the robots can do the basic washing, maybe the last people they keep are the ones who can handle the dying and the dementia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty a week is a lot on your pay. Where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership goes, that's fifteen. And I'd stop the streaming apps. Tomas will moan about the football, but he'd understand.

say: I'd say **care should stay human** and government should guarantee it.
I'd say **five years** is plenty of time to pass a law, so no excuses.
think: I think I'd **waste three years** hoping it won't happen.
I'd be **thirty-five** when robots come for the hands-on work in 2034.
do: Take the council's free **level three care diploma** to handle complex cases.
Save **twenty a week** by cutting the gym and streaming.
Attend union **campaign meetings**, not just read the emails.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, getting worse as the date gets closer.
S3.quote: Five years sounds long until you're in year four.
fieldNote: He's honest that he'd **delay acting**, which matches his dislike of change.
He'd learn more **care skills**, not technology, betting on complex and end-of-life work.
Even with time, **no savings** and few local jobs keep him alarmed.

steps.text: Enrol in the council's free level three care diploma
Cancel the gym and streaming to save twenty a week
Go to union campaign meetings in person

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when the robots arrive. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to make this fair, so let's use it. I'd push for a proper retraining fund paid for by the companies making the robots. That's something I could say anywhere without sounding like a crank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think ten years means I'd still be doing this job for most of it. The hands-on work is safe until about 2039. My worry is pay never improving, and then the jobs going just as I'm too old to start again easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing dramatic. I'd keep my rounds, do the level three diploma slowly, and get the car fixed properly so it lasts. I'd also talk to Tomas about whether we move nearer the town, where there's more than one agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm, but like I can breathe. The worry is still money, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving nearer the town: is that real or a maybe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A maybe. Tomas's mum is in the valley and he helps her with shopping. We'd only go if the rent was the same, and it never is. So probably we'd talk about it every year and not do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the decade warning enough to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it actually happen to the office first. If the rota and the paperwork go to AI around 2036 like they say, I'd believe the robots are three years behind. Until then it's just a story on the news.

say: I'd say we have **a decade** to make this **fair**, so use it.
I'd push for a **retraining fund** paid for by robot makers.
think: I think the **hands-on work** stays mine until about 2039.
My real worry is **pay never improving**, then jobs going when I'm forty.
do: Keep his rounds and do the **level three diploma** slowly.
Get the **car fixed properly** so it lasts for the rounds.
Talk with Tomas yearly about **moving nearer town**, where there are more agencies.
feel: **Calmer**, able to breathe, though money worry stays the same.
S4.quote: If the rota and the paperwork go to AI around 2036 like they say, I'd believe the robots are three years behind.
fieldNote: With ten years, his fear shifts from robots back to **stuck pay**.
He'd wait for **proof in the office** before believing the robot timeline.
Moving is talked about but **unlikely**, because of his partner's mother and rent.

steps.text: Keep the morning rounds and study the diploma part-time
Pay for a proper clutch repair so the car lasts
Watch whether office tasks go to AI before planning further

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. There's no time to save, no time to train, and nowhere else to go round here. What would help is a law that personal care stays with people, and until then, paid travel time and a mileage rate that covers the petrol.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the families. When the robots come, it won't just be my job, it'll be my client Mr Haddad sitting with a machine instead of someone who asks about his trains. I don't think anyone's asking him.

headlineQuote: When the robots come, it won't just be my job, it'll be my client Mr Haddad sitting with a machine instead of someone who asks about his trains.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old home care worker** driving an ageing hatchback between rural clients for a private agency.
He has about **two weeks' savings**, lives with his partner Tomas, and fears the car breaking down.
He is a **committed union member** who blames contract terms and wants laws, not gadgets.
He avoids technology and admits he would **wait too long** before acting on any warning.
His alarm peaks with **AGI by 2028** and eases only with a decade's notice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to save or train and few local jobs.
whatWouldHelp: A **law keeping personal care** with people.
Meanwhile, **paid travel time** and a mileage rate that covers petrol.
